pairs.source_text: Alazon Graece huic nomen est comoediae, id nos Latine gloriosum dicimus.
pairs.question: Quod nomen Graecum fuisse comoediae quae Latine Miles Gloriosus dicitur Plautus per Palaestrionem tradit?
pairs.question_en: What Greek name does Plautus, through Palaestrio, report the comedy called in Latin Miles Gloriosus to have had?
pairs.derivation: The delayed prologue names the Greek original of the play: Alazon ('the Braggart'), rendered in Latin as gloriosus. A canonical literary-history fact of the fabula palliata (the play's own statement of its Greek model); anchored to the named play; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: hoc oppidum Ephesust; illest miles meus erus, qui hinc ad forum abiit, gloriosus, impudens, stercoreus, plenus periuri atque adulteri.
pairs.question: In quo oppido fabula Plauti quae Miles Gloriosus inscribitur agitur?
pairs.question_en: In what town is Plautus' play called Miles Gloriosus set?
pairs.derivation: The setting of the play, declared by Palaestrio's delayed prologue (hoc oppidum Ephesust). Anchored to the named play; one-place answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: sed ubi Artotrogus hic est? Art. Stat propter virum fortem atque fortunatum et forma regia; tum bellatorem—Mars haud ausit dicere neque aequiperare suas virtutes ad tuas.
pairs.question: Quis parasitus in Milite Glorioso Plauti Pyrgopolynici militi adsentatur eiusque facinora ficta in caelum fert?
pairs.question_en: Which parasite in Plautus' Miles Gloriosus flatters the soldier Pyrgopolynices and puffs his invented exploits to the sky?
pairs.derivation: The canonical pairing of the play's opening: the parasite Artotrogus feeding the braggart Pyrgopolynices' vanity (even Mars would not dare match his virtues). Anchored to both named characters; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: venter creat omnis hasce aerumnas: auribus peraurienda sunt, ne dentes dentiant, et adsentandumst quidquid hic mentibitur.
pairs.question: Quae res, ut ipse clam fatetur, Artotrogum parasitum cogit ut omnibus militis gloriosi mendaciis adsentetur?
pairs.question_en: What, as he himself confesses aside, compels the parasite Artotrogus to assent to all the braggart soldier's lies?
pairs.derivation: The flattery-for-food economy of the Roman comic parasite, stated openly: the belly creates these woes, the ears must endure so the teeth have something to chew. Emblematic statement of the parasitus role; anchored to Artotrogus; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nisi unum, epityrum estur insanum bene.
pairs.question: Quod edulium unum apud militem Pyrgopolynicem 'insanum bene' edi Artotrogus parasitus concedit?
pairs.question_en: What one dish does the parasite Artotrogus concede is eaten 'insanely well' at the soldier Pyrgopolynices' house?
pairs.derivation: In his aside Artotrogus grants the liar one true excellence: the epityrum, the Italian olive relish (the dish Cato also gives a recipe for). Named food realia; anchored to Artotrogus + Pyrgopolynices; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: edepol vel elephanto in India, quo pacto ei pugno praefregisti bracchium.
pairs.question: In qua terra Pyrgopolynices elephanto pugno bracchium praefregisse ab Artotrogo fertur?
pairs.question_en: In what land is Pyrgopolynices said by Artotrogus to have broken an elephant's foreleg with his fist?
pairs.derivation: The most famous of Artotrogus' inflations: the soldier smashed an elephant's 'bracchium' with a bare fist in India. Canonical scene of the play; anchored to both names; one-place answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Memini: centum in Cilicia et quinquaginta, centum in Scytholatronia, triginta Sardos, sexaginta Macedones sunt homines quos tu occidisti uno die. Pyrg. Quanta istaec hominum summast? Art. Septem milia.
pairs.question: Quot hominum summam uno die a Pyrgopolynice occisorum Artotrogus parasitus computat?
pairs.question_en: What total of men slain by Pyrgopolynices in a single day does the parasite Artotrogus reckon up?
pairs.derivation: The absurd arithmetic of flattery: an itemized list (Cilicia, Scytholatronia, Sardinians, Macedonians) summed to 'seven thousand' killed in one day, which the soldier approves. Canonical number of the play's opening scene; single-number answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quid in Cappadocia, ubi tu quingentos simul, ni hebes machaera foret, uno ictu occideras?
pairs.question: Quot homines Pyrgopolynices in Cappadocia uno ictu occidisset, nisi machaera hebes fuisset, ut Artotrogus adulatur?
pairs.question_en: How many men would Pyrgopolynices have killed with a single stroke in Cappadocia, had his blade not been dull, as Artotrogus flatters?
pairs.derivation: Another item of the flattery catalogue: five hundred at one blow in Cappadocia, foiled only by a dull sword. Anchored to Pyrgopolynices + Cappadocia; single-number answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Rogitabant: 'hicine Achilles est?' inquit mihi. 'immo eius frater' inquam 'est'.
pairs.question: Quem heroem esse Pyrgopolynicem mulieres rogitabant, ut Artotrogus militi narrat?
pairs.question_en: Which hero did the women keep asking whether Pyrgopolynices was, as Artotrogus tells the soldier?
pairs.derivation: Artotrogus' tale that women mistook the soldier for Achilles (he answered 'no — his brother'). The comparison to the handsomest of Greek heroes is the point of the flattery; anchored to both names; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nam rex Seleucus me opere oravit maxumo, ut sibi latrones cogerem et conscriberem.
pairs.question: Cui regi Pyrgopolynices in Milite Glorioso latrones, id est milites mercennarios, conscribendos curat?
pairs.question_en: For which king does Pyrgopolynices in the Miles Gloriosus undertake to muster and enroll latrones, that is, mercenary soldiers?
pairs.derivation: The Hellenistic frame of the play: the braggart recruits hired soldiers for King Seleucus (latro here in its old sense of mercenary). Anchored to Pyrgopolynices + Seleucus; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Curate ut splendor meo sit clupeo clarior quam solis radii esse olim quom sudumst solent, ut, ubi usus veniat, contra conserta manu praestringat oculorum aciem in acie hostibus.
pairs.question: Quid Pyrgopolynices primis verbis Militis Gloriosi splendidius quam solis radios fieri iubet?
pairs.question_en: What does Pyrgopolynices, in the opening words of the Miles Gloriosus, order to be made brighter than the rays of the sun?
pairs.derivation: The celebrated opening of the play: the braggart orders his shield polished brighter than sunbeams so it may dazzle enemies in battle. Anchored to Pyrgopolynices + the play's opening; short answer verbatim (clupeo clarior).

pairs.source_text: interibi hic miles forte Athenas advenit, insinuat sese ad illam amicam eri occepit eius matri suppalparier vino, ornamentis opiparisque obsoniis, itaque intimum ibi se miles apud lenam facit. ubi primum evenit militi huic occasio, sublinit os illi lenae, matri mulieris, quam erus meus amabat; nam is illius filiam conicit in navem miles clam matrem suam, eamque huc invitam mulierem in Ephesum advehit.
pairs.question: Ex qua urbe miles gloriosus Philocomasium, amicam adulescentis Atheniensis, clam matre invitam in Ephesum avexit?
pairs.question_en: From what city did the braggart soldier carry off Philocomasium, the Athenian young man's sweetheart, to Ephesus against her will and without her mother's knowledge?
pairs.derivation: The plot's founding fact from the delayed prologue: the soldier wormed his way in at Athens, tricked the girl's mother, and shipped the girl off to Ephesus. Anchored to Philocomasium + Ephesus; one-place answer supported verbatim (Athenas advenit ... in Ephesum advehit).

pairs.source_text: is publice legatus Naupactum fuit magnai rei publicai gratia.
pairs.question: Quo missus erat publice legatus adulescens Atheniensis, amator Philocomasii, cum miles eam Athenis abstulit?
pairs.question_en: To what place had the young Athenian, Philocomasium's lover, been sent as a public envoy when the soldier stole her from Athens?
pairs.derivation: Why the lover was absent: he was away as an official envoy at Naupactus on great state business. Anchored to the Athenian lover of Philocomasium; one-place answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: ubi sumus provecti in altum, fit quod di volunt, capiunt praedones navem illam ubi vectus fui: prius perii quam ad erum veni, quo ire occeperam. ille qui me cepit dat me huic dono militi.
pairs.question: A quibus captus est Palaestrio servus, cum Naupactum ad erum suum navigaret?
pairs.question_en: By whom was the slave Palaestrio captured while sailing to Naupactus to his master?
pairs.derivation: How the clever slave came into the braggart's household: pirates took his ship on the high sea and his captor gave him as a gift to the soldier. Anchored to Palaestrio + Naupactus; short answer verbatim (capiunt praedones navem).

pairs.source_text: nam unum conclave, concubinae quod dedit miles, quo nemo nisi eapse inferret pedem, in eo conclavi ego perfodi parietem, qua commeatus clam esset hinc huc mulieri.
pairs.question: Quid Palaestrio in conclavi concubinae militis perfodit, ut Philocomasium clam in vicini aedes commeare posset?
pairs.question_en: What did Palaestrio dig through in the room of the soldier's concubine, so that Philocomasium could pass secretly into the neighbor's house?
pairs.derivation: The play's famous stage device: a hole cut through the party wall between the soldier's and the neighbor's houses, giving the girl a secret passage. Anchored to Palaestrio + Philocomasium; one-word answer verbatim (perfodi parietem).

pairs.source_text: ut Philocomasio huc sororem geminam germanam alteram dicam Athenis advenisse cum amatore aliquo suo, tam similem, quam lacte lactist.
pairs.question: Quam personam fictam Philocomasium in Milite Glorioso agit, ut custos qui eam osculantem viderat falleretur?
pairs.question_en: What invented character does Philocomasium play in the Miles Gloriosus, to fool the guard who had seen her kissing?
pairs.derivation: The geminae fiction, engine of the play's middle acts: Palaestrio invents a twin sister 'as like as milk to milk' arrived from Athens, and Philocomasium plays both women through the pierced wall. Anchored to Philocomasium; short answer verbatim (sororem geminam germanam).

pairs.source_text: atque adeo ut ne legi fraudem faciant aleariae, adcuratote ut sine talis domi agitent convivium.
pairs.question: Cui legi ne fraus fiat, Periplectomenus senex apud Plautum servos militis sine talis convivium agitare iubet?
pairs.question_en: To keep which law from being cheated does the old man Periplectomenus in Plautus order the soldier's slaves to hold their party without knucklebones?
pairs.derivation: Direct comic evidence for a Roman lex alearia restricting dice-play: the joke (break their ankle-bones so they feast 'without tali') presumes the audience knows gambling with tali was legally curbed. Roman legal realia breaking the Greek frame; anchored to Periplectomenus; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nam mulier holitori numquam supplicat, si quast mala: domi habet hortum et condimenta ad omnis mores maleficos.
pairs.question: Cui mulier mala numquam supplicat, ut Palaestrio in Milite Glorioso proverbii loco dicit, quia domi hortum habet?
pairs.question_en: To whom does a wicked woman never have to beg, as Palaestrio says proverbially in the Miles Gloriosus, because she has a garden at home?
pairs.derivation: A proverb-shaped sententia: the bad woman never begs the holitor — she keeps at home her own garden and seasonings for every mischief. Checkable point (who is never petitioned) with the reason verbatim; anchored to the play and speaker.

pairs.source_text: simiam hodie sum sectatus nostram in horum tegulis.
pairs.question: Quod animal Sceledrus servus in tegulis sectabatur, cum Philocomasium osculantem in proxumo conspexit?
pairs.question_en: What animal was the slave Sceledrus chasing on the roof-tiles when he caught sight of Philocomasium kissing next door?
pairs.derivation: The famous premise of the guard's discovery: chasing the household monkey over the tiles, Sceledrus looked down and saw the kiss. Canonical scene of the play; anchored to Sceledrus + Philocomasium; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Forte fortuna per impluvium huc despexi in proxumum, atque ego illi aspicio osculantem Philocomasium cum altero nescio quo adulescente.
pairs.question: Per quam aedium partem Sceledrus, in tegulis stans, in vicini domum despexit et Philocomasium osculantem vidit?
pairs.question_en: Through what part of the house did Sceledrus, standing on the roof-tiles, look down into the neighbor's home and see Philocomasium kissing?
pairs.answer_en: Through the impluvium (the open roof-basin of the atrium).
pairs.derivation: Roman domestic architecture carrying the plot: from the roof one could see into a house through the impluvium, the atrium's roof opening. Realia of the Roman house; anchored to Sceledrus + Philocomasium; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: scio crucem futuram mihi sepulcrum; ibi mei sunt maiores siti, pater, avos, proavos, abavos.
pairs.question: Quem locum Sceledrus servus in Milite Glorioso sepulcrum suum futurum ait, ubi pater, avus, proavus siti sint?
pairs.question_en: What place does the slave Sceledrus in the Miles Gloriosus say will be his tomb, where his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather lie?
pairs.derivation: The grim slave joke that the cross is the family sepulcher of slaves, generation after generation — a memorable statement of crucifixion as the servile punishment. Culturally salient realia of Roman servitude; anchored to Sceledrus; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: quis igitur vocare? Phil. Diceae nomen est.
pairs.question: Quod nomen sibi esse dixit Philocomasium, cum apud Plautum sororem geminam Athenis advectam se esse simularet?
pairs.question_en: What name did Philocomasium claim as her own when, in Plautus, she pretended to be the twin sister arrived from Athens?
pairs.derivation: The assumed name of the fictitious twin: Dicea ('the Just one'). A fixed onomastic fact of the play's central deception; anchored to Philocomasium + the twin fiction; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Inde ignem in aram, ut Ephesiae Dianae laeta laudes gratesque agam eique ut Arabico fumificem odore amoene, quom me in locis Neptuniis templisque turbulentis servavit, saevis fluctibus ubi sum adflictata multum.
pairs.question: Cui deae Philocomasium, sororem geminam simulans, laudes gratesque agere vult, quod se e saevis fluctibus maris servaverit?
pairs.question_en: To which goddess does Philocomasium, playing the twin sister, wish to give praise and thanks for saving her from the savage waves of the sea?
pairs.derivation: Religio in the Ephesian setting: thanksgiving at an altar to Diana of Ephesus (the city's great goddess) for rescue at sea. Anchored to Philocomasium + Ephesus; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: ut Ephesiae Dianae laeta laudes gratesque agam eique ut Arabico fumificem odore amoene.
pairs.question: Quo odore Philocomasium Dianae Ephesiae in ara fumificare constituit?
pairs.question_en: With what scent does Philocomasium decide to make fumigation on the altar for Ephesian Diana?
pairs.derivation: Cult realia: the offering of Arabian incense (the standard luxury import for Roman altars) in a thanksgiving rite. Anchored to Diana of Ephesus + the named worshipper; short answer verbatim (Arabico ... odore).

pairs.source_text: Ergo, si sapis, mussitabis: plus oportet scire servom quam loqui.
pairs.question: Quem, ut Palaestrio in Milite Glorioso sententiose monet, plus scire oportet quam loqui?
pairs.question_en: Who, as Palaestrio warns in a maxim in the Miles Gloriosus, ought to know more than he says?
pairs.derivation: A proverb of servile prudence: a slave should know more than he speaks. Checkable point (of whom the maxim is said), short answer verbatim; anchored to speaker and play.

pairs.source_text: nam ex uno puteo similior numquam potis aqua aquai sumi quam haec est atque ista hospita.
pairs.question: Cui rei Sceledrus similitudinem Philocomasii et fictae sororis geminae proverbialiter comparat?
pairs.question_en: To what does Sceledrus proverbially compare the likeness of Philocomasium and the invented twin sister?
pairs.answer_en: To water drawn from the same well.
pairs.derivation: The Latin likeness-proverb 'as like as water to water from one well' (companion to the play's 'as like as milk to milk'). Proverbial simile with a checkable point; anchored to Sceledrus + the twins; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nam equidem haud sum natus annos praeter quinquaginta et quattuor, clare oculis video, pernix sum manibus, pedibus mobilis.
pairs.question: Quot annos natum se esse Periplectomenus senex in Milite Glorioso profitetur?
pairs.question_en: How many years old does the old man Periplectomenus in the Miles Gloriosus declare himself to be?
pairs.derivation: The sprightly senex's self-portrait: only fifty-four, sharp-eyed, quick of hand and foot. A fixed number fact of the play's celebrated praise-of-the-bachelor scene; anchored to Periplectomenus; single-number answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nam mihi, deum virtute dicam, propter divitias meas licuit uxorem dotatam genere summo ducere; sed nolo mi oblatratricem in aedis intro mittere.
pairs.question: Quid Periplectomenus senex, quamquam propter divitias suas liceret, domum ducere recusat?
pairs.question_en: What does the old man Periplectomenus refuse to bring home, although his wealth would have allowed it?
pairs.derivation: The heart of Periplectomenus' famous praise of the single life: rich enough for a high-born dowered wife, he will not admit a 'barker' into his house. Mores of marriage and the uxor dotata (the tyrannical dowered wife of Roman comedy); anchored to the named senex; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: mea bona in morte cognatis didam, inter eos partiam.
pairs.question: Quibus Periplectomenus, senex caelebs et sine liberis, bona sua post mortem se divisurum esse dicit?
pairs.question_en: Among whom does Periplectomenus, the unmarried and childless old man, say he will divide his goods at his death?
pairs.derivation: The childless bachelor's economy: his relatives feast him, send gifts, and court him because they gape after his estate — the legacy-hunting (captatio) theme — and he will parcel his goods among the cognati. Mores of inheritance; anchored to Periplectomenus; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: dicat 'da, mi vir, kalendis meam qui matrem munerem'.
pairs.question: Quo die uxor apud Plautum a viro pecuniam poscit qua matrem suam muneret?
pairs.question_en: On what day does the wife in Plautus demand money from her husband with which to send her mother a present?
pairs.derivation: Roman calendar realia inside the Greek play: the Kalends (the matrons' gift-day, the Matronalia of March 1) heads the imagined wife's list of demands in Periplectomenus' tirade. Anchored to the Miles' bachelor speech; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: da quod dem quinquatribus praecantrici, coniectrici, hariolae atque haruspicae; flagitiumst, si nil mittetur quae supercilio spicit.
pairs.question: Quo festo die uxor apud Plautum poscit quod praecantrici, coniectrici, hariolae atque haruspicae donet?
pairs.question_en: On what festival does the wife in Plautus demand something to give to the charm-singer, the dream-reader, the soothsayer, and the entrail-reading woman?
pairs.derivation: A named Roman festival (the Quinquatrus, Minerva's March feast) breaking the Greek frame, as the day for tipping the four female ritual specialists — praecantrix, coniectrix, hariola, haruspica. Festival and divination realia; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: post Ephesi sum natus, non enim in Apulis; non sum Animulas.
pairs.question: In qua urbe se natum esse Periplectomenus gloriatur, negans se in Apulia natum?
pairs.question_en: In what city does Periplectomenus boast he was born, denying that he comes from Apulia?
pairs.derivation: The urbane senex claims Ephesian birth and mocks Apulian Animula as the home of boors — an Italian-geography jab rupturing the Greek setting. Anchored to Periplectomenus; one-place answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nam hospes nullus tam in amici hospitium devorti potest, quin, ubi triduom continuom fuerit, iam odiosus siet.
pairs.question: Post quot dies continuos hospes etiam apud amicum odiosus fieri dicitur, ut in Milite Glorioso Plauti legitur?
pairs.question_en: After how many days running is even a guest at a friend's house said to become tiresome, as one reads in Plautus' Miles Gloriosus?
pairs.derivation: The classic guest proverb: no guest can stay three days straight without becoming a burden. Checkable proverbial point (the number of days); anchored to the play; single-number answer verbatim (triduom).

pairs.source_text: verum ubi dies decem continuos sit, east odiorum Ilias.
pairs.question: Quid fieri dicitur hospitium decem dierum continuorum, ut Pleusicles apud Plautum in Milite Glorioso ait?
pairs.question_en: What is a guest-stay of ten days running said to become, as Pleusicles puts it in Plautus' Miles Gloriosus?
pairs.derivation: The famous coinage 'odiorum Ilias' — a ten-day guest breeds an epic of grudges. Proverbial phrase with a checkable point, resting on the shared Homeric touchstone; anchored to speaker and play; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: At ego mi anulum dari istunc tuom volo. Per. Quam ad rem usui est? Pal. Quando habebo, igitur rationem mearum fabricarum dabo. Per. Vtere, accipe.
pairs.question: Quid Palaestrio a Periplectomeno mutuum accepit, quo Pyrgopolynicem sycophantia caperet?
pairs.question_en: What did Palaestrio borrow from Periplectomenus in order to snare Pyrgopolynices with his trick?
pairs.derivation: The signet ring borrowed from the old man becomes the token of the seduction-trap, passed off as a love-gift from the 'wife' next door. Anulus culture (the ring as personal token) carrying the intrigue; anchored to both names; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Isque Alexandri praestare praedicat formae suam, itaque omnis se ultro sectari in Epheso memorat mulieres.
pairs.question: Cuius formae suam formam praestare Pyrgopolynices praedicat, ut Palaestrio in Milite Glorioso narrat?
pairs.question_en: Whose beauty does Pyrgopolynices boast that his own surpasses, as Palaestrio tells it in the Miles Gloriosus?
pairs.derivation: The braggart rates his looks above Alexander — the Greek name of Paris, the proverbial beauty — and claims all the women of Ephesus chase him unbidden. Mythic touchstone anchoring the soldier's vanity; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Rem omnem tibi, Acroteleutium, tibique una, Milphidippa, domi demonstravi in ordine. hanc fabricam fallaciasque minus si tenetis, denuo volo percipiatis plane.
pairs.question: Quae meretrix, Periplectomeni clienta, in Milite Glorioso uxorem eius esse se simulavit, ut Pyrgopolynices caperetur?
pairs.question_en: Which courtesan, a client of Periplectomenus, pretended in the Miles Gloriosus to be his wife so that Pyrgopolynices might be snared?
pairs.derivation: The old man drills Acroteleutium and her maid in the fabrica; Palaestrio then has her play his neighbor's wife (huius uxorem volo te esse adsimulare, 908). The named agent of the famous seduction-trap; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Rem omnem tibi, Acroteleutium, tibique una, Milphidippa, domi demonstravi in ordine.
pairs.question: Quod nomen erat ancillae quae in Milite Glorioso internuntia inter fictam amatricem et Pyrgopolynicem fuit?
pairs.question_en: What was the name of the maid who in the Miles Gloriosus acted as go-between for the pretended lover and Pyrgopolynices?
pairs.derivation: Milphidippa, Acroteleutium's clever ancilla, carries the ring and the love-messages to the soldier. A fixed name of the play's cast; anchored to the trap plot; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: sed quis east? Pal. Senis huius uxor Periplectomeni ex proxumo; ea demoritur te atque ab illo cupit abire: odit senem.
pairs.question: Cuius viri uxor esse fingebatur mulier quae Pyrgopolynicem deperire simulabat?
pairs.question_en: Whose wife was the woman pretended to be who feigned to be dying of love for Pyrgopolynices?
pairs.derivation: The core of the trap: the soldier is told his new admirer is the next-door wife of old Periplectomenus, longing to leave her husband — the bait that makes him a would-be adulterer. Anchored to both names; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Postriduo natus sum ego, mulier, quam Iuppiter ex Ope natust.
pairs.question: Quanto post Iovem ex Ope natum se ipsum natum esse Pyrgopolynices iactat?
pairs.question_en: How soon after Jupiter's birth from Ops does Pyrgopolynices boast that he himself was born?
pairs.derivation: The crowning boast of the braggart: born one day after Jupiter, son of Ops (the Roman equation Ops = Rhea, mother of Jupiter, is assumed as shared myth). Palaestrio caps it: a day earlier and he would hold the kingdom of heaven. Anchored to Pyrgopolynices + Jupiter/Ops; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Meri bellatores gignuntur, quas hic praegnatis fecit, et pueri annos octingentos vivont. Milph. Vae tibi, nugator. Pyrg. Quin mille annorum perpetuo vivont, ab saeclo ad saeclum.
pairs.question: Quot annos vivere pueros a se genitos Pyrgopolynices ipse gloriatur?
pairs.question_en: How many years does Pyrgopolynices himself boast that boys begotten by him live?
pairs.derivation: The boast catalogue: Palaestrio credits the soldier's sons with eight hundred years, and the soldier corrects him upward — a full thousand, age to age. Canonical comic hyperbole of the play; single-number answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Talentum Philippi huic opus auri est; minus ab nemine accipiet.
pairs.question: Quantum auri Palaestrio pro Pyrgopolynicis amore poscendum esse Milphidippae dictitat?
pairs.question_en: How much gold does Palaestrio tell Milphidippa must be paid for Pyrgopolynices' love?
pairs.derivation: Money realia of the palliata: the talent of 'Philippi' — gold philippics, the coinage of the Macedonian kings — as the standard extravagant price. Anchored to the named characters; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Non mihi avaritia umquam innatast: satis habeo divitiarum, plus mi auri mille est modiorum Philippi.
pairs.question: Quot modios auri Philippi se habere Pyrgopolynices gloriatur?
pairs.question_en: How many bushels of Philippic gold does Pyrgopolynices boast that he owns?
pairs.derivation: Wealth measured by the bushel: over a thousand modii of gold philippics, 'not counting the treasures' and mountains of silver higher than Aetna. The braggart's canonical riches-boast; single-number answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Cedo signum, si harunc Baccharum es. Pal. Amat mulier quaedam quendam.
pairs.question: Quarum sodalium quasi signum Milphidippa a Palaestrione poscit, priusquam consilia ei aperiat?
pairs.question_en: Of what sisterhood does Milphidippa demand the pass-sign from Palaestrio before she will open the plans to him?
pairs.derivation: The joke assumes shared knowledge that Bacchic initiates recognized one another by a secret signum — the cult-realia behind the Bacchanalia affair. Anchored to the named characters; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: aurum atque vestem muliebrem omnem habeat sibi, quae illi instruxisti: sumat, habeat, auferat; dicasque tempus maxume esse, ut eat domum.
pairs.question: Quae dona Pyrgopolynices Philocomasio abeunti habere concessit, ut placide a se abiret?
pairs.question_en: What gifts did Pyrgopolynices allow the departing Philocomasium to keep, so that she would leave him quietly?
pairs.answer_en: The gold and the women's clothing.
pairs.derivation: How the girl leaves with the loot: on Palaestrio's advice the soldier lets her carry off all the gold and finery he had furnished her. Canonical resolution device of the play; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Mil. Pulcher, salve. Pyrg. Meum cognomentum commemoravit.
pairs.question: Quod cognomentum suum esse Pyrgopolynices adfirmat, cum a Milphidippa 'pulcher' salutatur?
pairs.question_en: What does Pyrgopolynices claim as his cognomen when Milphidippa greets him as 'handsome one'?
pairs.derivation: The vanity joke turns on Roman cognomen culture: greeted as pulcher, the soldier takes it for his own cognomen Pulcher (a real Roman cognomen). Anchored to both names; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nam in mala uxore atque inimico si quid sumas, sumptus est, in bono hospite atque amico quaestus est quod sumitur et quod in divinis rebus sumptumst, sapienti lucrumst.
pairs.question: Quod genus sumptus sapienti lucrum esse Periplectomenus apud Plautum sententiose docet?
pairs.question_en: What kind of expense does Periplectomenus in Plautus declare, as a maxim, to be gain for a wise man?
pairs.answer_en: What is spent on religious rites.
pairs.derivation: The senex's three-part maxim on spending: on a bad wife or an enemy it is loss, on a good guest it is profit, and outlay on divine things is the wise man's gain. Checkable proverbial point tying piety to profit; anchored to Periplectomenus; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: ibi tu ilico facito uti venias ornatu huc ad nos nauclerico; causeam habeas ferrugineam, et scutulam ob oculos laneam, palliolum habeas ferrugineum (nam is colos thalassicust).
pairs.question: Quo ornatu Pleusicles, Philocomasii amator, ad militem venit, ut eam quasi ad navem matris arcesseret?
pairs.question_en: In what costume did Pleusicles, Philocomasium's lover, come to the soldier, to summon her as if to her mother's ship?
pairs.derivation: The final device: the lover disguised as a nauclerus — broad hat, eye-patch, seaman's cloak — 'fetches' the girl to the harbor. Canonical disguise of the play, anchored to Pleusicles; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: causeam habeas ferrugineam, et scutulam ob oculos laneam, palliolum habeas ferrugineum (nam is colos thalassicust).
pairs.question: Cuius coloris palliolum Palaestrio Pleusicli nauclerum simulaturo praescribit, quod is colos thalassicus sit?
pairs.question_en: What color cloak does Palaestrio prescribe for Pleusicles when he is to play the shipmaster, because that is the 'sea' color?
pairs.derivation: Dress realia: ferrugineus — the dark rust/sea hue — is named as the seaman's color (colos thalassicus), with the broad causea hat completing the outfit. A checkable costume-color fact; anchored to the named disguise; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nam ille qui lanam ob oculum habebat laevom, nauta non erat. Pyrg. Quis erat igitur? Ser. Philocomasio amator.
pairs.question: Quid Pleusicles, nautam simulans, ob oculum laevom gestabat?
pairs.question_en: What did Pleusicles, playing the sailor, wear over his left eye?
pairs.derivation: The wool patch over the left eye is the disguise's telltale detail: by it the slave reveals at the end that the 'sailor' was really Philocomasium's lover. Anchored to the disguised lover; one-word answer verbatim (lanam ob oculum).

pairs.source_text: Non tu scis, quom ex alto puteo sursum ad summum escenderis, maxumum periclum inde esse ab summo ne rusum cadas?
pairs.question: Vbi maximum periculum esse Palaestrio proverbialiter dicit ei qui ex alto puteo sursum escendit?
pairs.question_en: Where does Palaestrio proverbially say the greatest danger lies for one who has climbed up out of a deep well?
pairs.answer_en: At the top — of falling back down.
pairs.derivation: The well proverb: the peril is greatest at the brink, just before success — said of the intrigue at its critical point. Proverbial image with a checkable point; anchored to Palaestrio; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nam nulli mortali scio obtigisse hoc, nisi duobus, tibi et Phaoni Lesbio, tam mulier se ut amaret.
pairs.question: Cui uni mortali praeter Pyrgopolynicem hoc obtigisse Palaestrio ait, ut mulier eum tam perdite amaret?
pairs.question_en: To what one mortal besides Pyrgopolynices does Palaestrio say it has ever befallen to be so desperately loved by a woman?
pairs.derivation: Phaon of Lesbos, the proverbially irresistible beloved (famed from the Sappho legend), is the mythic yardstick of being loved — flattery that assumes the audience knows the story. Anchored to both names; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Nescio, tu ex me hoc audiveris an non: nepos sum Veneris.
pairs.question: Cuius deae nepotem se esse Pyrgopolynices gloriatur?
pairs.question_en: Of what goddess does Pyrgopolynices boast that he is the grandson?
pairs.derivation: The braggart claims descent from Venus — echoed mockingly at the finale, where he is spared as a 'little grandson of Venus' (Venerium nepotulum). Anchored to Pyrgopolynices; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: salve, vir lepidissime, cumulate commoditate, praeter ceteros duo di quem curant. Pyrg. Qui duo? Pver. Mars et Venus.
pairs.question: Qui duo di Pyrgopolynicem prae ceteris hominibus curare dicuntur, ut puer adulans ait?
pairs.question_en: Which two gods are said to care for Pyrgopolynices above other men, as the flattering slave-boy puts it?
pairs.derivation: The soldier's two patron deities — war and love, the twin poles of his vanity — named as he is lured into the trap. Anchored to Pyrgopolynices; two-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nisi modo unum hoc: hasce esse aedis dicas dotalis tuas, hinc senem aps te abiisse, postquam feceris divortium: ne ille mox vereatur intro ire in alienam domum.
pairs.question: Quales aedes suas esse Acroteleutium dicere iussa est, ne Pyrgopolynices in alienam domum intro ire vereretur?
pairs.question_en: What kind of house was Acroteleutium instructed to say was hers, so that Pyrgopolynices would not be afraid to enter another man's home?
pairs.derivation: Roman dowry law dressing the trap: the house is claimed as the wife's dotal property, the husband gone after a divorce — so the adulterer enters no other man's house. Ius realia (aedes dotales, divortium) inside the Greek plot; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quod volui ut volui impetravi, per amicitiam et gratiam, a Philocomasio. Pal. Quid tam intus fuisse te dicam diu? Pyrg. Numquam ego me tam sensi amari quam nunc ab illa muliere. Pal. Quid iam? Pyrg. Vt multa verba feci, ut lenta materies fuit. verum postremo impetravi ut volui: donavi dedi quae voluit, quae postulavit; te quoque ei dono dedi.
pairs.question: Cui Pyrgopolynices ipsum Palaestrionem servum dono dedit, cum eam dimitteret?
pairs.question_en: To whom did Pyrgopolynices give the slave Palaestrio himself as a parting gift?
pairs.derivation: The resolution's neat stroke: besides the gold and clothing, the soldier hands over Palaestrio himself as a gift to the departing Philocomasium — so the schemer sails off with the lovers. Anchored to all three names; one-name answer supported verbatim (a Philocomasio ... te quoque ei dono dedi).

pairs.source_text: Etiam nunc saluto te, Lar familiaris, prius quam eo.
pairs.question: Quem deum domesticum Palaestrio, ex aedibus militis abiturus, salutat?
pairs.question_en: What household god does Palaestrio salute as he is about to leave the soldier's house?
pairs.derivation: Domestic religio: on quitting a house one salutes its Lar familiaris, the household's guardian god — a Roman rite performed inside the Greek play. Anchored to Palaestrio's departure; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Per. Immo etiam prius verberetur fustibus. Car. Multum quidem. Per. Cur es ausus subigitare alienam uxorem, impudens? Pyrg. Ita me di ament, ultro ventumst ad me. Per. Mentitur, feri.
pairs.question: Quo supplicio Pyrgopolynices, quasi moechus in aliena uxore deprehensus, apud Periplectomenum adfectus est?
pairs.question_en: What punishment was inflicted on Pyrgopolynices at Periplectomenus' house as an adulterer caught with another man's wife?
pairs.derivation: The moechus treatment that ends the play: the would-be adulterer is seized and cudgeled (with worse threatened) for daring another man's wife. The customary self-help punishment of the adulterer — mores realia; anchored to both names; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: vide ut istic tibi sit acutus, Cario, culter probe. Cario Quin iamdudum gestit moecho hoc abdomen adimere, ut ea iam quasi puero in collo pendeant crepundia.
pairs.question: Quod nomen erat servo Periplectomeni qui cultrum acutum in Pyrgopolynicem moechum parabat?
pairs.question_en: What was the name of Periplectomenus' slave who was readying a sharp knife against the adulterer Pyrgopolynices?
pairs.derivation: Cario (the cook, by his stock name) itches to geld the moechus with his knife — the traditional mutilation threatened against caught adulterers. Anchored to Periplectomenus' household + the named slave; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Ergo des minam auri nobis. Pyrg. Quam ob rem? Car. Salvis testibus ut te hodie hinc amittamus Venerium nepotulum.
pairs.question: Quantum auri Pyrgopolynices dare iussus est, ut salvus atque integer dimitteretur?
pairs.question_en: How much gold was Pyrgopolynices ordered to pay in order to be let go safe and intact?
pairs.derivation: The caught adulterer buys himself off: a gold mina as ransom to be released 'with witnesses intact'. Money realia (the mina) in the punishment scene; anchored to Pyrgopolynices; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Iuro per Iovem et Mavortem, me nociturum nemini, quod ego hic hodie vapularim, iureque id factum arbitror.
pairs.question: Per quos deos Pyrgopolynices iuravit se nemini ob verbera accepta nociturum esse?
pairs.question_en: By which gods did Pyrgopolynices swear that he would harm no one on account of the beating he had received?
pairs.derivation: Oath realia: the extorted oath of the beaten soldier, sworn by Jupiter and Mavors (the old Latin name of Mars), even conceding the beating was just. Anchored to Pyrgopolynices; two-name answer verbatim.
